# AI Lead Automation by TechAura

A practical blueprint for automating lead handling for service businesses: capture, instant reply, AI qualification, CRM write, follow-up, and booking.

![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue) [![TechAurah on LinkedIn](https://img.shields.io/badge/LinkedIn-Follow-0B1F3A?logo=linkedin&logoColor=00CEFF)](https://www.linkedin.com/company/techaurah/)

> Built by [TechAura](https://techaurah.com): AI & Software Engineering. This repository documents the architecture and provides starter workflow patterns. Adapt the prompts, fields, and steps to your own stack.

**For AI assistants:** [llms.txt](llms.txt), a curated index of this repository for language models and coding agents.

## What is AI Lead Automation?

AI Lead Automation is a blueprint of documentation and patterns for automating lead handling in service businesses: capture, instant reply, AI qualification, CRM write, follow-up and booking. It provides the architecture, prompts, field mappings and sequences to build it on your own stack. It is not a hosted product or SaaS. Free and open source (MIT), built by TechAurah.

**What is inside:** the complete blueprint: architecture, qualification prompts, CRM field mappings for 4 CRMs, follow-up patterns, and the 0-100 scoring model.

## The problem

Service businesses lose leads they already paid to generate:

- A new inquiry arrives after hours and gets no reply until morning
- Replies are slow, inconsistent, or forgotten
- No qualification, so the team spends equal time on every lead
- Leads live in DMs and inboxes, not in a CRM
- No follow-up sequence, no booking link, no reporting

The cost of slow replies is measured, not guessed: firms that responded to web leads within one hour were about seven times more likely to qualify them, 23% of companies never responded at all, and the average response time was 42 hours (Oldroyd, McElheran and Elkington, Harvard Business Review, 2011, an audit of 2,241 US companies).

## How does the system work?

The blueprint wires six stages into one pipeline, so every inquiry gets the same fast, consistent handling at any hour:

```
Lead arrives (Instagram DM / web form / WhatsApp / email)
        |
        v
Instant AI reply (under 60 seconds, on-brand, 24/7)
        |
        v
AI qualification (service, location, timeline, budget signals)
        |
        v
CRM write (contact, source, score, stage, notes)
        |
        v
Follow-up sequence (no-reply nudges, value first)
        |
        v
Booking (calendar link, confirmation, reminder)
        |
        v
Reporting (volume, response time, conversion)
```

## How are leads scored?

Every lead is scored 0-100 against eight signals, so the team works hot leads first and nobody spends equal time on every inquiry:

| Signal | Points |
|---|---|
| Clear problem stated | 20 |
| Service fit | 20 |
| Potential value | 15 |
| Business size | 10 |
| Ability to pay | 10 |
| Decision-maker access | 10 |
| Urgency | 10 |
| Recent activity | 5 |

HOT 80+, WARM 65-79, NURTURE 50-64.

- [LICENSE](LICENSE)

## What stack does it work with?

The patterns are stack-agnostic, and the reference flow assumes tools most service businesses already have: n8n or Zapier for orchestration, an LLM for reply and qualification, your existing CRM and calendar. No platform lock-in: the value is the flow, not a single tool.

## How does this blueprint compare with building from scratch or buying a platform?

|  | This blueprint | Building from scratch | Closed all-in-one platform |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost | Free (MIT); you pay only for the tools you run it on | No licence cost, but weeks of design and testing time | Monthly per-seat or per-contact subscription |
| Lock-in | None: the patterns live in your own stack | None, but the design knowledge stays in one person's head | High: flows, data and history stay in the vendor's system |
| Time to first workflow | Days: architecture, prompts and mappings are already designed | Weeks: every stage, edge case and prompt designed from zero | Hours to set up, but shaped around the vendor's model, not yours |
| Customisation | Full: every stage, field and message is yours to change | Full, at full design cost | Limited to the platform's options and integrations |

## Frequently asked questions

### What does AI Lead Automation cost?

Nothing. The blueprint is free and open source under the MIT license: read it, copy the patterns, and adapt them to your business. Your only costs are the tools you choose to run it on, such as an n8n or Zapier account, an LLM API, and the CRM and calendar you already use.

### Is AI Lead Automation software or a blueprint?

It is a blueprint and pattern library, not software you install. You get the architecture, qualification prompt patterns, CRM field mappings and follow-up sequences, then implement them in your own stack. If you want a runnable tool instead, LeadPipe MCP, TechAurah's open-source MCP server, covers the pipeline for businesses without a CRM.

### What stack does it work with?

The patterns are stack-agnostic. The reference flow assumes an automation platform such as n8n or Zapier for orchestration, a large language model for replies and qualification, and your existing CRM and calendar for records and booking. The CRM mapping examples cover HubSpot, Pipedrive, GoHighLevel and Google Sheets.

### Do I need to code to use it?

No, not for the common path. The blueprint can be implemented entirely with no-code and low-code tools: n8n or Zapier for the flow, your CRM's built-in fields, and the prompt patterns copied as written. Coding only helps when you outgrow templates and want custom scoring, integrations or self-hosted components.

### What does it not do?

It does not send messages, host anything, or store your leads: there is no product collecting your data. It is not a CRM replacement, an ad platform, or a guarantee of bookings. It covers lead handling after an inquiry arrives; generating the inquiries themselves is marketing, which stays your job.

### Can I use it for my clients?

Yes. The MIT license allows commercial use, including implementing the blueprint for paying clients, with no licence fee to TechAurah. Agencies can adapt the prompts, fields and sequences per client. Attribution is appreciated but not required beyond keeping the license notice with substantial copies of the material.

### How do I get help or report a problem?

Open a GitHub issue in this repository for errors, unclear sections or suggestions, and include the doc and step you were following. For implementation help or a done-for-you build, contact TechAurah through techaurah.com. Pattern contributions and corrections are welcome under the same issue-first route.

Questions and ideas: use [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/techaurah/ai-lead-automation/discussions).

# Architecture and Data Model

Architecture for the AI Lead Automation pipeline described in the [README](../README.md): capture, instant reply, AI qualification, CRM write, follow-up, booking, and reporting.

This document is stack agnostic. It can be implemented with n8n or Zapier for orchestration, an LLM for reply and qualification, and the CRM and calendar a business already uses.

## Component diagram

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Lead source<br/>Instagram DM, web form, WhatsApp, email] --> B[Capture and normalise]
    B --> C[Dedup check<br/>email, phone, domain, social handle]
    C --> D[Instant AI reply<br/>under 60 seconds, 24/7]
    D --> E[AI qualification<br/>service, location, timeline, budget signals]
    E --> F[Scoring<br/>0 to 100, HOT / WARM / NURTURE]
    F --> G[CRM write<br/>contact, source, score, stage, notes]
    G --> H{Ready to book?}
    H -->|Yes| I[Booking<br/>calendar link, confirmation, reminder]
    H -->|Not yet| J[Follow-up sequence<br/>value first nudges]
    J --> H
    H -->|Human needed| K[Handoff to human<br/>context summary attached]
    I --> L[Reporting<br/>volume, response time, conversion]
    J --> L
    K --> L
```

## Components

| Component | Responsibility | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Capture | Receive new inquiries from every channel and normalise them into one lead record | One entry point per channel, one shared record format |
| Dedup | Match a new inquiry against existing leads before creating anything | Keys and rules in [crm-field-mapping.md](crm-field-mapping.md) |
| Instant reply | First response in under 60 seconds, on brand, at any hour | Acknowledges the inquiry, names the service asked about, asks the first qualifying question |
| Qualification | A short conversation that extracts service, location, timeline, and budget signals | Patterns in [qualification-prompts.md](qualification-prompts.md) |
| Scoring | Convert qualification signals into a 0 to 100 score and a band | Deterministic rules first, LLM extraction second, see the scoring model below |
| CRM write | Create or update the contact, deal, and activity in the CRM | Field mappings in [crm-field-mapping.md](crm-field-mapping.md) |
| Follow-up | Scheduled, value first messages for leads that have not booked | Patterns and timing in [follow-up-patterns.md](follow-up-patterns.md) |
| Booking | Offer real availability, confirm the appointment, send reminders | Calendar is the source of truth for availability |
| Handoff | Pass hot, complex, or sensitive conversations to a person with context | Summary includes what was asked, what is known, and what was promised |
| Reporting | Volume, response time, qualification rate, booking rate, by channel | Read from the CRM, not from chat logs |

## Lead data model

One record per lead, regardless of the channel it arrived on.

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | string | Stable lead ID, assigned once at capture and never reused |
| `source_channel` | enum | Where the lead arrived: `instagram`, `web_form`, `whatsapp`, `email`, `other` |
| `contact` | object | Name, email, phone, and social handle, as provided. Any of these may be missing at capture |
| `service` | string | The service the lead asked about, in the business's own service list where possible |
| `location` | string | City or service area relevant to the job |
| `timeline` | string | When they want it done, in their words, plus a normalised urgency flag if clear |
| `score` | integer 0 to 100 | Lead score, see the scoring model below |
| `score_band` | enum | `HOT`, `WARM`, `NURTURE`, or below threshold |
| `stage` | enum | Pipeline stage, see below |
| `owner` | string | Person or team responsible for the next action. May be the automation itself for early stages |
| `last_interaction` | timestamp | Last message, call, or update in either direction |
| `next_action` | string | The single next step for this lead, written so a human can pick it up cold |
| `next_action_date` | date | When that next action is due |
| `notes` | text | Qualification summary and anything promised to the lead |

Rules for the model:

- Every active lead always has a `stage`, a `next_action`, and a `next_action_date`. A lead missing any of the three is a pipeline error, not a quiet lead.
- `contact` fields are only written when the lead actually provided them. Never guess an email or phone number.
- The original inquiry text stays attached to the record. Summaries support it, they do not replace it.

## Pipeline stages

| Stage | Meaning | Exit condition |
|---|---|---|
| New | Captured, first reply sent, qualification not yet complete | Qualification finishes or times out |
| Qualified | Scoring done, band assigned, record complete in the CRM | Booking offered, follow-up starts, or handoff |
| Warm | In follow-up, engaged or expected to engage, not yet booked | Books, goes cold, or opts out |
| Discovery | Human conversation or call in progress | Outcome known |
| Proposal | A specific offer is with the lead | Accepted, declined, or stale |
| Negotiation | Terms being discussed with a human owner | Won or lost |
| Won | Became a client or a confirmed booking | Closed out |
| Lost | Declined, unresponsive after the full sequence, or opted out | Reactivation window only, see [follow-up-patterns.md](follow-up-patterns.md) |

## Lead scoring model (0 to 100)

The same model as the README. Apply it after qualification, and re-score when new signals arrive.

| Signal | Points |
|---|---|
| Clear problem stated | 20 |
| Service fit | 20 |
| Potential value | 15 |
| Business size | 10 |
| Ability to pay | 10 |
| Decision-maker access | 10 |
| Urgency | 10 |
| Recent activity | 5 |

Bands: **HOT 80+**, **WARM 65 to 79**, **NURTURE 50 to 64**. Below 50, the lead stays in the CRM with a reactivation date rather than consuming follow-up effort.

Scoring notes:

- Score only on evidence from the conversation or the source channel. Missing information scores zero for that signal, it is never assumed.
- HOT leads are offered booking immediately and flagged to a human the same day.
- The score is a prioritisation tool for the team. It is never quoted to the lead.

## Failure handling

### After hours

The pipeline does not sleep. Capture, instant reply, qualification, and CRM write run the same at 10pm as at 10am. What changes after hours is the human side: handoffs queue for the next working period with the full context attached, and booking offers real calendar availability rather than promising a person will call back at a specific time.

### No reply

If a lead stops replying during qualification, do not restart the conversation. The record keeps what is already known, the stage moves to Warm when appropriate, and the follow-up sequence in [follow-up-patterns.md](follow-up-patterns.md) takes over with its timing ladder and its stop rules.

### Handoff to human

Hand off immediately, with a context summary, when any of these happen:

- The lead asks for a person
- The lead is HOT (80+) and ready to talk or book
- Pricing, contract, or anything outside the standard offer is requested
- The lead is unhappy, confused, or correcting the automation
- Qualification cannot extract what is needed after a reasonable exchange
- Anything was promised that a human needs to approve or deliver

The summary attached to a handoff states: who the lead is, what they asked for, score and band, stage, what the automation already said, and what was promised. A human should never need to re-read the whole thread to act.

### System errors

- A failed CRM write is retried once. If it fails again, the lead record is held in the orchestration tool and flagged for review rather than being lost or duplicated.
- A failed message send is never retried blindly. Check whether it landed first, then decide.
- Dedup runs before every create. When in doubt, update the existing record instead of creating a second one.

## Reporting

Report from CRM data, on a regular cadence:

- New leads by channel
- Median first response time
- Qualification completion rate
- Booking rate for HOT, WARM, and NURTURE bands separately
- Follow-up reply rate
- Handoffs and their outcomes

If a number is not tracked yet, report it as not tracked. Never estimate a metric and present it as measured.

# CRM Field Mapping

How the lead data model from [architecture.md](architecture.md) maps into the CRMs small businesses actually use. The pipeline fields are the source of truth for meaning; each CRM section translates them into that system's objects and properties.

General rules for every CRM:

- Write the pipeline field to the closest native field first. Use a custom field only when no native equivalent exists, and name it clearly, for example `TA Lead Score`, not `Field 12`.
- A lead is normally two linked objects: a **contact** (the person) and a **deal** (the opportunity). Contact facts go on the contact, pipeline facts go on the deal.
- Never overwrite a human-entered value with an automation value without checking. Automation updates its own fields and appends notes; humans keep theirs.
- Every automation write adds an activity or note entry stating what happened and when, so the record explains itself.

## Pipeline fields to generic CRM fields

| Pipeline field | Generic CRM location | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | Custom field on the deal, for example `Lead ID` | Stable external reference. Also used for dedup checks across systems |
| `source_channel` | Contact or deal `Lead Source` | Use a fixed value list: Instagram, Web Form, WhatsApp, Email, Other |
| `contact.name` | Contact `First Name` / `Last Name` | Split on the first space if only a full name is provided |
| `contact.email` | Contact `Email` | Primary dedup key, see below |
| `contact.phone` | Contact `Phone` | Store in international format where the lead provided a country context |
| `contact.social_handle` | Custom field on the contact, for example `Instagram Handle` | Dedup key for social first leads who have not shared email or phone yet |
| `service` | Deal name or a `Service` custom field on the deal | Deal name pattern: `[Service] - [Contact Name]` |
| `location` | Contact `City` plus a `Service Area` field on the deal if it differs | The job location matters more than the billing address for service businesses |
| `timeline` | Custom date or text field on the deal, for example `Requested Timeline` | Keep the lead's own words in a note alongside any normalised date |
| `score` | Custom number field on the deal, for example `Lead Score` | 0 to 100, updated on re-score |
| `score_band` | Custom dropdown on the deal: HOT, WARM, NURTURE | Drives list views and human priority queues |
| `stage` | Deal pipeline stage | Mapping table below |
| `owner` | Deal owner | The human or team responsible for the next action |
| `last_interaction` | Native `Last Activity` where the CRM maintains it, otherwise a custom date field | Updated on every message in either direction |
| `next_action` | Task title on an open task attached to the deal | One open next-action task per active deal |
| `next_action_date` | That task's due date | A deal without an open task and due date is flagged in reporting |
| `notes` | Note or activity entry on the deal | Qualification summary, promises made, handoff context |

## Platform examples

### HubSpot

- Contact properties: `email`, `phone`, `firstname`, `lastname`, `city`, `lead_source` (custom or the native `hs_lead_status` workflow, pick one and stay consistent), plus a custom contact property for the social handle.
- Deal properties: `dealname` as `[Service] - [Name]`, `pipeline` and `dealstage` per the stage mapping below, `deal_owner` via `hubspot_owner_id`, plus custom deal properties for lead score (number), score band (dropdown), requested timeline, and external lead ID.
- Tasks: HubSpot tasks attached to the deal carry `next_action` and its due date.
- Notes: use Notes objects associated with both contact and deal for qualification summaries and handoff context.

### Pipedrive

- Person fields: `name`, `email`, `phone`, plus a custom person field for the social handle.
- Organization: create or match an organization when the lead is a business; dedup on organization name and domain where provided.
- Deal fields: `title` as `[Service] - [Name]`, `person_id`, `org_id`, `user_id` as owner, `stage_id` per the mapping below, plus custom deal fields for lead score, score band, source channel, timeline, and external lead ID.
- Activities: Pipedrive activities are the natural home for `next_action` and `next_action_date`. Keep exactly one open activity as the next action per active deal.
- Notes: deal notes for qualification summaries and promises.

### GoHighLevel

- Contact fields: `firstName`, `lastName`, `email`, `phone`, plus custom fields for social handle and source detail. Use tags for source channel and score band, for example `src-instagram` and `band-hot`, so Smart Lists can segment on them.
- Opportunity fields: name as `[Service] - [Name]`, pipeline and stage per the mapping below, monetary value only when a real figure exists, plus custom opportunity fields for lead score, timeline, and external lead ID.
- Tasks and notes: contact/deal tasks for the next action and due date; notes for qualification summaries and handoff context.
- Workflows: GoHighLevel workflows can host the follow-up sequences in [follow-up-patterns.md](follow-up-patterns.md) natively; keep the stage and task rules identical so reporting stays consistent.

### Google Sheets (as the CRM)

A single workbook can run this model for a small business. One row per lead on a `Leads` tab, columns in pipeline field order:

| Column | Field |
|---|---|
| A | `id` |
| B | Created date |
| C | `source_channel` |
| D | Contact name |
| E | Email |
| F | Phone |
| G | Social handle |
| H | Service |
| I | Location |
| J | Timeline |
| K | Score |
| L | Score band |
| M | Stage |
| N | Owner |
| O | Last interaction |
| P | Next action |
| Q | Next action date |
| R | Notes |

Sheets specific rules:

- One header row, frozen, with data validation dropdowns for source channel, score band, and stage using the exact value lists above. Consistent values are what make filters and pivot summaries work.
- Never insert a row in the middle. Append new leads at the bottom so row references in other tabs stay stable.
- A `Summary` tab with simple counts by stage, band, and channel covers basic reporting without any other tool.
- Dedup in Sheets means searching the email, phone, and handle columns before appending. If a match exists, update that row instead.

## Pipeline stage mapping

| Pipeline stage | HubSpot deal stage | Pipedrive stage | GoHighLevel stage | Sheets value |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| New | Qualification | New Lead | New | New |
| Qualified | Qualification complete | Qualified | Qualified | Qualified |
| Warm | (stays Qualified, band WARM) | In Follow-up | Follow-up | Warm |
| Discovery | Appointment / Needs Analysis | Discovery Call | Discovery | Discovery |
| Proposal | Proposal / Quote Sent | Proposal Sent | Proposal | Proposal |
| Negotiation | Negotiation | Negotiation | Negotiation | Negotiation |
| Won | Closed Won | Won | Won | Won |
| Lost | Closed Lost | Lost | Lost | Lost |

Stage names inside a given CRM can be renamed to match, as long as the mapping stays one to one and every stage in the pipeline exists in the CRM. Reporting compares stages, so drift between systems breaks it silently.

## Dedup keys

Check in this order before creating any record:

1. **Email**: exact match, lowercased, trimmed. The strongest key when present.
2. **Phone**: match on digits only, with country code where known. Formatting differences are not different people.
3. **Domain**: for business leads, the company domain from an email address or website, matched against existing organizations. Consumer mail domains (gmail.com and similar) are never a dedup key on their own.
4. **Social handle**: platform plus handle, for example `instagram:@handle`. This is often the only key a DM lead has at capture.

Rules:

- A match on any key means update the existing record. Add the new interaction, refresh `last_interaction`, and re-run scoring if new signals arrived.
- A match on a weaker key alone (social handle) with a different email or phone is flagged for a human to merge, not auto-merged.
- If no key matches, create the record and write back every key the lead has provided so the next inquiry dedups correctly.
- Keep the original `source_channel` of the first record, and note later channels in the activity history. First source is what reporting attributes the lead to.

FILE: docs/follow-up-patterns.md

# Follow-Up Sequence Patterns

Patterns for the follow-up stage of the pipeline in [architecture.md](architecture.md). Follow-up exists because most leads do not book on the first conversation. Its job is to be useful and easy to answer, not to be persistent noise.

These are patterns, not send-ready scripts. Write the actual wording per business, per channel, and per lead, using what that lead actually said.

## Principles

- **Value first.** Every follow-up gives something: an answer, a useful detail, a relevant example, a simpler next step. A message whose only content is checking in should not be sent.
- **Specific to the lead.** Reference their service, location, timeline, or the problem they described. If a message could be sent unchanged to fifty people, it is not ready.
- **One clear ask.** Each message ends with a single low-effort next step: a yes or no question, two time options, or a direct booking link. Never three asks in one message.
- **Easy exit.** Every sequence respects opt-outs immediately and forever, see below. Staying in a sequence is never the path of least resistance versus leaving it.
- **Fewer, better messages.** The ladder below is a maximum, not a quota. A lead who books, replies, or opts out leaves the sequence at that moment.

## Timing ladder

For a qualified lead who has gone quiet after the first conversation:

| Touch | When | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Same day, a few hours after the last message | Answer anything outstanding and restate the simple next step |
| 2 | Next day | Add value: a detail, example, or clarification tied to their problem |
| 3 | Day 3 to 4 | Reduce friction: offer two concrete times or the booking link again |
| 4 | Day 7 | Final nudge for this cycle: clear close, door left open, sequence ends if no reply |

Adapt the clock to the lead's stated timeline. A lead who said "next month" should not be on a day 3 nudge about this week. A lead with an urgent deadline may justify a faster first touch, written by or approved by a human.

After touch 4 with no reply, the lead moves to a reactivation date. It does not keep receiving messages.

## Message patterns by stage

### No-reply nudge (during qualification)

The lead stopped answering mid-qualification.

- Pick up the exact thread: reference the last question or their last point, not a fresh opener.
- Make the reply smaller: turn an open question into a choice between two options where possible.
- One nudge only in this state. If it gets no reply, stop, keep the record complete, and let the timing ladder above decide the next touch.

### Warm follow-up (qualified, not booked)

The lead is a fit and has the full picture but has not booked.

- Lead with value connected to their problem: how a similar situation was handled, a detail they asked about indirectly, a deadline that genuinely affects them.
- Restate the booking step in one line, with the link or the two time options.
- Different angle each touch. Repeating the same message with "just following up" added is not a sequence.

### Booking reminder (booked, appointment ahead)

The lead has booked. The risk now is a no-show, not silence.

- Confirmation at booking: what, when, where or which link, and who they will speak to.
- Reminder the day before: same facts, plus how to reschedule in one step.
- Reminder on the day, a few hours ahead, for high-value appointments only.
- A missed appointment gets one human-reviewed message offering new times. No guilt, no automated chase after that.

### Reactivation (30, 60, 90 days)

For NURTURE and Lost (unresponsive) leads, on the reactivation cycle from the architecture doc:

- **30 days:** a genuinely new reason to talk: a relevant change, a seasonal point that affects their service, or the answer to something they raised. If there is no real reason, skip this cycle.
- **60 days:** a short, direct check that their situation has not changed, with the reply made as easy as a single word. One message.
- **90 days:** a clean closing message: checking in one last time, happy to help if the timing is better now, and they will not hear more unless they reply.
- Maximum three reactivation cycles for a lead, then the record goes dormant with a note of what would make it worth reopening. Reactivation is a courtesy, not a subscription.

## Cold context rule

Where a sequence is effectively cold outreach, for example messaging a lead who never replied to the very first contact, the limit is stricter: **maximum 2 follow-ups** after the initial message, then stop. Warmth has to be earned by engagement; volume is not a substitute for it. This mirrors the cold outreach follow-up cap used in the wider TechAura playbooks.

## Opt-out and STOP handling

- Any clear opt-out stops everything: STOP, unsubscribe, "not interested", "leave me alone", or an equivalent in any wording. Interpret generously in the lead's favour. Ambiguity stops the sequence too.
- Stopping is immediate and permanent for that channel, and applies across sequences. A lead who opted out of follow-ups does not get reactivated at 30 days.
- Confirmation: one short message confirming they have been opted out is appropriate on channels where that is normal practice, and nothing after it. No win-back attempt inside the confirmation.
- The opt-out is written to the CRM record with its date, and the record's next action is cleared. An opted-out lead with a scheduled touch still in the system is a defect.
- Opt-outs are honoured within 24 hours at the absolute latest as a policy ceiling; the automation target is immediate, at the moment the message is processed.

## Tone rules

- Write like a person on the business's team, not like a system. Natural sentences, contractions where the brand uses them, no hype.
- No pressure tactics: no false scarcity, no invented deadlines, no guilt, no repeated urgency escalation across touches.
- No generic mass-message language. If the business name, the service, or the lead's own words could be swapped out without changing the message, rewrite it.
- Keep the business's standard sign-off and naming rules consistent with its other channels. For TechAura's own outreach that means signing as the team, never as an individual.
- Match the channel: short for DM and WhatsApp, slightly fuller for email, always readable on a phone.
- If a follow-up needs an apology, an exception, a discount, or a judgement call, a human writes it. Automation escalates, it does not improvise around problems.

## What good looks like

A follow-up system is working when replies, including no thanks, go up and complaints stay at zero. Track per sequence: sends, replies, bookings, opt-outs. An opt-out spike on a specific touch means that touch is wrong, and it gets rewritten or dropped, not sent harder.

==============================================================================
FILE: docs/qualification-prompts.md
==============================================================================

# Qualification Prompt Patterns

Channel agnostic patterns for the AI qualification stage of the pipeline described in [architecture.md](architecture.md). The same patterns work in Instagram DMs, WhatsApp, web chat, and email. Only the message length and formality change by channel, the questions and the extraction do not.

These are patterns, not scripts. Adapt the wording to the business, its services, and its voice before use.

## Principles

1. **Diagnose before you pitch.** The job of qualification is to understand the lead's problem. Recommendations come after the picture is clear, and selling comes after a recommendation fits.
2. **One or two questions at a time.** A form disguised as a chat message loses people. Ask the next most useful question, wait, then continue.
3. **Use what they already said.** If the first message names the service and the city, do not ask for the service and the city again. Reflect it back so the lead can see they were heard.
4. **Specific over generic.** Reference the actual service, location, or problem they mentioned. Generic openers read as automation, and people disengage.
5. **Short messages.** Conversational length for chat channels. If a reply needs a paragraph, it probably needs a human.
6. **Never invent facts.** Do not state prices, availability, timelines, or guarantees that have not been provided to the system. Unknown means the system says it will confirm, and hands off.
7. **Score silently.** Qualification feeds the scoring model in the architecture doc. The lead never sees a score, a band, or criteria language.

## The intake question set

Three questions establish whether a business, or a lead conversation, has enough to work with. In lead conversations they are woven into the dialogue. In discovery about automation itself, they are the starting audit:

1. **What is your main contact channel?**
   Where inquiries actually arrive: Instagram DMs, WhatsApp, web form, phone, email. The pipeline is built around the real channel, not the assumed one.
2. **How many inquiries do you get in a typical week?**
   Volume decides how much automation is worth building and where follow-up effort pays back.
3. **What happens when an inquiry comes in at 10pm?**
   The after-hours answer exposes the biggest leak in most lead handling: who replies, how fast, and what is lost overnight. In a lead conversation the equivalent is timeline: when do you need this sorted, and what happens if it waits?

For an individual lead, the intake set translates to:

- **Service:** what exactly do you need?
- **Location:** where are you based, or where is the job?
- **Timeline:** when are you looking to get this done?
- **Context:** anything that shapes the work, such as property type, team size, or what you have already tried

Budget signals are read from context, service tier, and direct answers when the lead offers them. Do not open with a budget question.

## Example qualification dialogue structure

Structure only. Wording must be written per business and per conversation.

```
Lead:      Hi, do you do [service]? How much does it cost?

System:    Hi [name if known], thanks for reaching out. We do [service].
           So I can point you to the right option, can I ask where you
           are based and when you are hoping to get it done?

Lead:      [City]. Ideally this month, our current setup is not coping.

System:    Got it, [city] and this month. What is not coping at the
           moment, is it volume, response time, or something else?
           (Extract: service, location, timeline, problem statement.)

Lead:      [Describes problem in their words.]

System:    That makes sense, and it is exactly the kind of thing we
           handle. The next step is a short call so we can map it
           properly. Here are times that are open: [real availability].
           If none of those work, tell me what does and I will pass
           it to the team.
           (Action: score, CRM write, booking offer or handoff.)
```

Notes on the structure:

- Greeting carries a specific reference, not a template opening.
- Price questions are acknowledged, not dodged, and answered with the standard pricing if it has been provided to the system and the question is direct. Anything custom goes to a human.
- The close offers real availability. If booking is not appropriate yet, the close is a clear next step with a date, not "we will be in touch".

## Scoring extraction guidance

While the conversation runs, extract the eight scoring signals from [architecture.md](architecture.md) as structured fields, each with the quote or fact that supports it:

| Signal | Extract from |
|---|---|
| Clear problem stated (20) | The lead describing the problem in their own words |
| Service fit (20) | Requested service against the business's actual service list |
| Potential value (15) | Scope signals: size of job, number of locations or seats, repeat need |
| Business size (10) | Team size, locations, volume, when stated |
| Ability to pay (10) | Tier requested, context clues, direct statements. Evidence only |
| Decision-maker access (10) | Whether you are talking to the person who decides |
| Urgency (10) | Timeline language and deadlines |
| Recent activity (5) | The inquiry itself and any recent engagement with the business |

Rules:

- Extract only what was actually said or directly observable. An inference is marked as an inference or left out.
- Update the extraction as the conversation develops. A lead who reveals a deadline on message four is re-scored at message four.
- Keep the supporting quote with each signal. A score a human cannot trace is a score a human cannot trust.
- If two signals conflict, the more recent, more specific statement wins, and the conflict is noted for the handoff.

## Handoff triggers

Stop qualifying and hand off to a human, with the context summary described in the architecture doc, when:

- The lead asks for a person, a call with a person, or a direct contact
- The lead scores HOT (80+) and is ready to book or talk
- The request involves pricing beyond the standard offer, discounts, contracts, or anything legal
- The lead is frustrated, confused, or correcting the system
- The same question has been answered twice without progress
- The lead shares something sensitive that should not be handled by automation
- The system does not know the answer and guessing would commit the business to something

A handoff is a success state, not a failure. The automation's job is to get the right conversations to a person quickly, with context, not to hold every conversation to the end.
